title: Effects of Heavy Strength Training on Running Performance and Determinants of Running Performance in Female Endurance Athletes
authors: Vikmoen O, Raastad T, Seynnes O, Bergstrøm K, Ellefsen S, Rønnestad BR
population: 19 well-trained female endurance athletes (VO2max 53 +/- 3 ml/kg/min, 5.8 h of endurance training a week), randomised to endurance training alone (n = 8) or endurance plus strength training (n = 11)
findings: The strength training was four leg exercises of 3 sets of 4-10 repetition maximum, twice a week for 11 weeks, added to normal endurance training.

The strength group raised leg-exercise 1RM by 40 +/- 15% and counter movement jump height by 6 +/- 6% and squat jump height by 9 +/- 7% (p < 0.05), with larger fibre cross-sectional area in the vastus lateralis (type I 13 +/- 7%, type II 31 +/- 20%) and no change in capillary density or patellar tendon stiffness.
Neither group changed running economy, fractional utilisation of VO2max or VO2max, and neither changed the distance run in a 40-minute all-out test.
The authors conclude that adding heavy strength training to endurance training did not affect 40-minute all-out running performance or running economy compared with endurance training only.
limitations: Nineteen women in two small groups; one test of running performance (a 40-minute all-out run) and a laboratory economy test; the athletes were endurance athletes in general (the abstract does not say how many were runners); 11 weeks. A null result in a small sample is not proof of no effect. Abstract read; full text not read.
implications: The one women-only randomised trial in the corpus whose abstract reports running economy found large strength gains and no gain in economy or in a 40-minute run. It does not by itself overturn the pooled economy effect (a statement about those analyses that this abstract does not make), but it is a reason to word the benefit as 'may' and to say that the evidence in women is small.
Pairs with the same group's trial in female duathletes (vikmoen-2017-female-duathletes-strength), where performance improved after prolonged submaximal work.
